1. Designing small-scale pretraining: backward from the evaluation

children.label: 1. Designing small-scale pretraining: backward from the evaluation

children.value: Large-scale pretraining is outside the scope of this repository. But
small-scale pretraining, like the small MLM of module 01 notebook 02, is knowledge needed to read every pretraining paper.
Decide the evaluation and the split first.

Decide the downstream task and the held-out split, and only then build the pretraining data. The homology-cluster-level split seen in module 01 is an example. If you reverse the order, the evaluation sequences get mixed into the pretraining. It is a problem seen repeatedly in modules 04 and 05.

Sequences in public DBs over-represent close relatives. If you sample in a balanced way from the clusters made with an identity threshold, you can see more diverse sequences with the same compute†. Which threshold favors downstream differs by task, so decide it by experiment.

(Micikevicius et al. 2017) is, per the abstract, a method that trains in half precision while keeping a single-precision copy of the weights and scaling the loss. bf16 often does not need loss scaling†. (§4). In the position-block split, the mean order in all three assays was probe ≥ full > LoRA. DN7A is 0.56/0.54/0.41, IF1 is 0.43/0.38/0.22, A0A is 0.28/0.24/0.14, and the number of seeds in which LoRA was higher than the probe is 0 of 9. In the random split, full fine-tuning was the same as or slightly higher than the probe (in IF1, in all 3 seeds, by about +0.05). This is a result obtained with about 1 thousand training variants, an 8M model and fixed settings.

(§4). In the random split, B2, which uses the position one-hot, is the same as or higher than fine-tuning and the probe, at 0.81 on DN7A and 0.66 on A0A. In the position-block split, B1 is higher than the ESM-2 probe’s 0.56 and 0.28, at 0.61 on DN7A and 0.40 on A0A. Only on IF1 does the probe lead B1 (0.43 vs 0.22), but the seed variation is large. Before saying “ESM is better than the baseline”, always include a baseline that uses the position effect (module 02).
The ranking and the size change with the split

(§4). The random scores of the ESM-based methods are 0.61–0.82, much higher than the 0.14–0.56 of position-block. Every method fluctuates a lot in the problem of predicting new positions. The per-seed values of IF1 and A0A are spread from −0.10 to 0.60. With 3 seeds it is hard to settle the ranking between methods.
The LoRA result depends strongly on the setting

(§6). The default setting fixed in advance (r=8, lr 1e-3) was 0.385, the second lowest of the 6 LoRA settings, and the full range was 0.29–0.50. In seeds 0–1, every LoRA setting was lower than the probe’s 0.56. However, this is the result of a limited search over settings, and since validation-based selection (exercise 2) was not done, we do not conclude that LoRA is worse. For full fine-tuning, the default lr 5e-5 was the best, and it got worse, 0.452, at lr 2e-4. When it was re-run on a Colab T4, this ranking changed: the default setting was the lowest of the 6, and lr 3e-3 was 0.430 (§8).
The order can flip with scale

(§6). The result of looking at DN7A with the 35M model and the position-block split (2 seeds) was LoRA 0.57 ≥ full 0.53 ≥ probe 0.49, a different order from 8M. Even so, it did not exceed the B1 of the same seeds, 0.59 and 0.61. There are only 2 seeds, so we do not generalize to “LoRA is better at 35M”. Also, the 0.49 of the 35M frozen probe was lower than the 0.56 of the 8M probe of the same seeds. A larger model does not always mean a better frozen representation.
There are things LoRA reduces and things it fails to reduce

(§5). The trainable parameters are 61,761, only 0.83% of the full 7,409,402. However, the training time for the same number of steps fell by only 11–12% at 8M and 24–25% at 35M. This is because the gradient computation of the frozen weights is skipped but backpropagation through the activations remains as it is. How much it shrinks depends on the model structure and the implementation. With 5 epochs fixed, the last-epoch training loss on DN7A was 0.278 for LoRA, higher than the 0.163 of full fine-tuning. In this setting it may be underfitting. That the output of the initial LoRA model is exactly the same as the original, with a maximum absolute difference of 0, was confirmed in the implementation check.
There are only two models, 8M and 35M, and 35M was used on only one assay. It uses 3 short proteins and trains a randomly initialized linear head

as the backbone. LP-FT, which trains only the head first, or initializing the head with a zero-shot score, was not tried†. The large gradients of the initial head may have damaged the pretrained representation and worked against fine-tuning. There are 3 seeds, and 2 for 35M and the sensitivity experiments. The training data is about 1 thousand; the epochs and LR were fixed in advance and only a small sensitivity analysis was looked at, with no validation-based tuning and no intervals computed. It does not represent the results of larger models, more data and well-tuned fine-tuning. Biderman 2024’s “LoRA learns less and forgets less” is a claim in an LLM setting, so these results can neither verify nor refute it.

children.value: The 7,397 human Swiss-Prot proteins are split into 5,917 train and 1,480 Pfam-group test, and 83 keywords are used. The model is ESM-2 35M and the SAE is a TopK SAE with dictionary 3,840 and k=32. The values in the table are the
of the per-keyword test AUROC, and the brackets are the Pfam-group bootstrap 95% interval. The features are chosen on train and measured on test.

The pre-specified primary comparisons are written as the difference of the medians with the 95% interval, and the number of keywords where the SAE was higher. At layer 6, SAE − original dimensions is +0.022 [+0.016, +0.053] and it was higher on 53 of the 83 keywords. SAE − random dictionary is +0.022 [+0.015, +0.049] and 58. At layer 12, SAE − original dimensions is +0.037 [+0.016, +0.056] with 52, and SAE − random dictionary is +0.028 [+0.014, +0.042] with 52. The reconstruction error FVU of the SAE is 0.145 at layer 6 and 0.195 at layer 12, and for the random dictionary 0.745 and 0.747, respectively.
The SAE reconstructs well, but reconstruction is not interpretability
(§3). It explains 80–85% of the variance, while the random dictionary reaches only 25%. But concept alignment must be measured separately.
There is a gain, but it is small

in the table, SAE − original dimensions is +0.047 at layer 6 and +0.037 at layer 12, and SAE − random dictionary is +0.021 and +0.038, respectively. The pre-specified comparison that first computes the per-keyword differences and then takes their

is +0.02–0.04 as in the paragraph above, and the interval does not include 0. The SAE is higher on 63–70% of the keywords. But it is far from the 0.83 of the supervised probe. A single unsupervised feature cannot be the whole representation of a concept.

(§5). The untrained random dictionary is similar to or slightly higher than the original dimensions (0.657 and 0.631 at layer 6), and PCA is similar too, at 0.645 and 0.665. When it was re-run on Colab, PCA at layer 12 was 0.694, 0.03 higher than the random dictionary, so “PCA ≈ random dictionary” was not reproduced (§8). If you pick the best on train out of thousands of candidates, the median train AUROC of 0.74–0.78 falls to 0.63–0.70 on test. The drop is 0.08–0.14 depending on the method and layer. The SAE went down from 0.784 to 0.678 at layer 6, and from 0.782 to 0.701 at layer 12. However, the rules for choosing the candidates differ. For the SAE the candidates are 3,840 positive directions, and for the original dimensions and PCA they are 480 directions in both signs. Only the random dictionary is a control with the same number of candidates and the same rule as the SAE. Hard keywords fell below chance level on test. Deafness fell from 0.66 on train to 0.45 on test, and Lipid-binding from 0.69 to 0.42.
For easy concepts, it fits well even without training

(§6). At layer 12, the best SAE features are GTP-binding 0.99, Signal 0.99 and Transmembrane 0.98. But the random dictionary also gets 0.97, 0.94 and 0.93, and the original dimensions 0.95, 0.80 and 0.85. Even when all of the top 5 test proteins have the keyword, if they are one family, like 5 RHO GTPases or 5 SLC35 transporters, they are not 5 independent pieces of evidence.
Individual features hardly corresponded across seeds

(§6). Comparing the decoder directions of two SAEs that differ only in seed on the same data, the median nearest cosine was 0.312. Between random dictionaries it is 0.162, and only 0.8% of the features had a cosine of 0.9 or more. Yet the median keyword AUROC was similar for the two seeds, 0.713 and 0.701. With 2 seeds and the nearest cosine alone, you cannot assert either “the aggregate performance is stable” or “the features are reproduced”. This is because the nearest cosine is not evidence of a one-to-one correspondence or of functional equivalence. The reconstruction FVU is 0.195 and it is a small-scale 12-epoch setting, so the effect of undertraining may also be there.
There were no dead features, and the activation density is skewed

(§4). If counted by the protein-level max, every feature looks on and the metric becomes meaningless, so we recounted with 1,893,297 residues as the unit. Both the SAE and the random dictionary had 0% dead features. The mean density of TopK is k/F, that is 0.83%, but for the SAE the median density is 0.29% at layer 6 and 0.43% at layer 12, and the top 1% of features are on in 11% and 8% of the residues, so the distribution is skewed. The random dictionary had medians of 0.69% and 0.66%, and top 1% of 2.9% and 3.3%. This means that “high-density” features that are on very often are mixed in with the concept features.

(§2). It is a calculation without the activations, not a measurement, and is based on pure fp32 AdamW. Full fine-tuning a 650M model with fp32 AdamW needs about 10.4 GB. When a result comes out in which the frozen probe beats LoRA and full fine-tuning, what should you check before concluding that fine-tuning is “useless”?

You must check five things. First, were the settings fixed in advance? In the LoRA sensitivity of notebook 01, results under the same conditions fluctuated between 0.29 and 0.50. Second, were early stopping or the LR chosen on a validation basis? That was not done here. Third, how large is the training data? It is small, about 1 thousand. Fourth, how many seeds? In the position-block split the per-seed values fluctuated from −0.10 to 0.60. Fifth, what is the split? In the random split, full fine-tuning was the same as or slightly higher than the probe. So "it did not lead in this fixed setting and this split" is the accurate statement.
What does LoRA reduce and what does it fail to reduce? Answer with the numbers of the notebook.

The trainable parameters shrink, in the 8M model, to 61,761, which is 0.83% of the full 7,409,402. The optimizer state and the gradient memory shrink accordingly (the formula of §2). However, only the gradient computation of the frozen weights is skipped, and backpropagation through the activations remains. So the training time fell by only 11–12% at 8M and 24–25% at 35M. How much is saved depends on the model structure and the implementation. Also, the last-epoch training loss was higher for the same number of steps, which may be underfitting.
Why does the position one-hot (B2) come out similar to or higher than the ESM-2 probe in the random split, and what does that imply?

In the random split, other substitutions at the same position are in train, so the per-position mean effect can be used. This is because the one-hot columns of B2 have learned values at the test positions too. In the position-block split that information is absent, so B2 becomes similar to B1 (DN7A from 0.81 to 0.61). There are two implications. The gain of ESM in the random split is overestimated unless you compare it with a baseline that uses the position effect. And to predict new positions, you need a split like position-block.
Why must you not look at the sensitivity table of notebook 01, pick the best LoRA setting and report its test score? How should that table be used?

If you choose the setting by the test score, you get an optimistic value fitted to the test set. It is the same principle as the layer choice in module 04. Choose the setting on a validation split inside the training data, split in the same way as the outer split. Use the sensitivity table only to report how much the conclusion depends on the setting (exercise 2).
Why is a random-dictionary control needed in the evaluation that matches SAE features with keywords? What did this module show?

Because if you pick the one that fits best on train from thousands of candidates, even a meaningless direction looks good by chance — a selection effect arises. The median test AUROC of the untrained random TopK dictionary at layer 12 was 0.663, similar to 0.664 for the original dimensions, and the SAE was +0.028 [+0.014, +0.042] higher than that. The empirical difference from this particular random control, +0.028, is small. And how much of the SAE's gain comes from the overcomplete sparse readout itself and how much from training cannot be decomposed by this experiment alone. There were also keywords such as Deafness and Lipid-binding in which the feature that was the best on train fell below chance level on test.
What can be said, and what cannot be said, from the observation that “feature 2564 turns on in GTP-binding proteins”? How would you see causation?

One thing can be said. The activity of this feature shows a high correlation with the keyword, an AUROC of 0.99, on held-out proteins. Three things cannot be said. That the model *uses* that feature for judging GTP binding, that the feature points to only one concept (the top 5 are one family, so the generality is also limited), and that the same feature is reproduced when the seed is changed (median nearest cosine 0.31). To see causation, you must measure how the downstream prediction changes when the contribution of the feature is removed (ablation), compared with the case where a random feature is removed (exercise 4).
The median keyword AUROCs of two SAEs that differ only in seed were similar, but the individual feature directions hardly corresponded. How should the interpretation be written?

The aggregate performance was similar in the two seeds, but with only 2 seeds the stability cannot be asserted. The individual directions of the dictionary hardly corresponded, and the nearest cosine itself does not guarantee a one-to-one correspondence or functional equivalence. So do not assert that "feature number N is concept X". Instead, report the correspondence across several seeds and the change with dictionary size and sparsity together, and write as limitations whether the reconstruction is sufficient (FVU 0.195, 12 epochs) and the possibility of undertraining. Do not generalize the result of this one setting.
Why can training be wrong even when the parameter hashes of all the ranks are the same in DDP? How do you check?

DDP averages the gradients so that all the ranks make the same update. This equivalence itself holds only under conditions such as even shards, the same initial values and stochastic operations turned off. However, even when the data is split wrongly — for example, when there is no sampler and all the ranks see the same samples — the parameters across the ranks are the same as one another. In notebook 03, the hash of the run without the sampler was also the same. But the maximum absolute difference from the single process that used the same global batch was 4.7e-4, about 120,000 times larger than the 3.7e-9 of normal DDP. To check, compare the parameters with a single process run with the same global batch and seed.
You want to release the LoRA weights fine-tuned in this module. List three or more things to check before releasing.

First, check the license of the base model and the license of the training data. ESM-2 is stated as MIT, but you must check the notice obligations†. ProteinGym's repository code is MIT, but for the DMS data you must check the original source per assay, and this repository could not confirm it. Second, write the training data and split, the limitations (about 1 thousand variants, 3 assays) and the usage restrictions in the model card. Third, review dual use. Look at whether the functions that these weights enable could be misused, and decide the scope of release and the access-control options (Baker & Church 2024, Sandbrink 2023). Fourth, check your institution's policy and review requirements. Fifth, record the revision, seeds and environment for reproduction. This is not legal advice.
